For the north face at fixed x, as z decreases the column stays constant and the row moves downward, so the north face traces a vertical line. That means at a given image column, moving downward should trace through one of these faces depending on which surface is actually in view.

Following a specific column, the top edge line sits at roughly v≈u+2, and below that lies the north face, matching the darker region I identified earlier. I'm now trying to pin down where the lighter region falls by checking specific column values to see which row range it corresponds to.

So I'm reconsidering—maybe the lighter region is actually the dimly lit top face, and the darker region is the shadowed north face, with the boundary between them marking the top edge rather than the lighter region's start.

The boundary positions I'm tracking (u384→~441, u416→488, u448→beyond frame) don't line up cleanly, so I'm now wondering if the very dark region is actually a separate object in front rather than part of the mass's north face.

A constant v=415 corresponds to constant x on the top face — computing D from v gives x≈2.70, meaning there's a horizontal edge at that x value spanning u372-400, with corresponding y ranging roughly from 7.55 to 7.62. Checking the ratio (u-256)/(v-256) along the bottom boundary shows it's not quite constant, shifting from about 0.63 at u372 to 0.70 at u420, so it's not a simple linear relationship after all.

This kind of back-projection reasoning is getting too deep without visual confirmation — I should just look at the actual image instead of continuing to infer geometry blindly. With 36 frames left in the budget, I want to be efficient, but understanding this NE region matters, so it's worth reading the image directly. My hunch is that dark object (22,24,25) in the NE pocket could be an entirely new object that wasn't present before, distinct from the mass spanning u246-511 seen earlier at position (1.300,7.400).

I'm also second-guessing whether the gray-blue mask I found in obs_0162 actually captured that dark region, since (22,24,25) has too small a blue-red difference to be caught by that filter — meaning what I found there was something else. The cheapest way to resolve this is to just read the pixel values from obs_0164 and cross-check against obs_0162 directly.
